extracted.intended_audience: current or aspiring chairs of university mathematics departments (or similar academic department chairs)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical operational and managerial guidance for chairs of mathematics departments: handling faculty (stars, part-timers, retirees), resources (library, computers, endowed chairs), fundraising, and interacting effectively with the Dean. Focused on everyday decisions and departmental strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling celebrity faculty / 'prima donna' management
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a highly distinguished or 'fancy' faculty member who commands attention and resources, you must balance their special status with fairness to the rest of the department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange resources so the celebrity's compensation/perks do not starve the rest of the faculty—ideally by getting an endowed Chair Professorship so the salary and perks come from the Dean's/Endowment budget rather than the departmental budget. Use limited departmental raise money to care for other deserving faculty. Be aware the celebrity may feel mistreated and seek outside offers; this is a balancing act that may require negotiating with the Dean and deciding how to allocate scarce discretionary funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to outside offers for faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: When a faculty member brings an outside job offer, decide ethically how to respond, balancing dignity, retention, and limited authority to make counter-offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect full details of the competing offer (salary, perks, spouse/kids considerations, what's special about the other school). A gentlemanly competitive counter-offer is appropriate, but you will usually need the Dean's cooperation because you don't control checks. Use discretionary departmental funds where possible (temporary raises, teaching-load adjustments, travel funds) if the Dean refuses to counter. Recognize many outside offers are partly for attention; sometimes a civilized counter-offer can retain the person, but if the offer is to the candidate's 'dream institution' you may be unable to compete. Tailor the response to the prestige/attractiveness of the outside school (e.g., Harvard/Princeton gives you leverage; a tiny regional college may not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Library stewardship and advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the department's library resources (books, journals, interlibrary arrangements, and liaison librarian) meet the scholars' needs and are ordered and funded appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for a well-funded, up-to-date math collection and, if possible, a dedicated Math Library or a strong relationship with the Math Librarian. Appoint a faculty librarian/committee member to oversee orders but keep the Chair's 'finger on the pulse'. Understand modern complexities (electronic resources, journal bundling) and maintain good communication with the Math Librarian to make informed purchase decisions. Be mindful interlibrary loan delays can stall research or teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Securing computer support and technology funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and fund the department's evolving computer and network needs, including hardware, high-speed Internet, printers/scanners, and technical staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the case to the Dean that computers and technicians are ongoing entitlements (maintenance, salaries) rather than one-off purchases. Consider creative funding (soft-money grants in allied departments, hiring through grants temporarily) when Dean funding is scarce. Budget for annual equipment replacements and for a full-time technician where appropriate; note that many deans balk at continuing salary commitments, so prepare persuasive arguments and possibly external justification (e.g., shared support from other departments or grant offsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring and managing part-time faculty ('freeway fliers')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use part-time instructors to cover heavy undergraduate and service teaching obligations while understanding the trade-offs in quality, pay, and departmental integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that modern math departments often cannot cover large teaching loads with tenure-track faculty alone. Hire part-time faculty for service courses (precalculus, calculus, stats) with awareness of low per-course pay and limited perks. Some part-timers have year-long contracts and are more stable; others teach at multiple institutions (freeway fliers). Treat part-timers humanely where possible, but understand institutional politics (some deans prefer regular faculty teaching all courses). Note that part-timers sometimes achieve better teaching evaluations than highly-paid regular faculty; use that fact in discussions with the Dean. Be aware of limits on providing staff support, offices, and participation in governance for part-timers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursuing and managing endowed Chair Professorships
rubrics_metrics.description: Endowed Chairs are high-status positions paid from endowments; obtaining them benefits the department by removing cost from the departmental budget and enhancing prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand what an endowed Chair typically includes: special salary, reduced teaching load or special courses, discretionary funds, possibly a personal secretary and invitations to events. Endowed Chairs cost roughly $2–4 million to establish (varies). Use development office expertise to solicit donors and aim to get Chairs to reach parity with other departments. Recognize Chairs belong to the Dean/university, not the department; when a Chairholder retires, the Chair returns to the Dean's pool. Accept that donor preferences may skew to more visible fields (Medicine, Chemistry) and plan fundraising accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing retirement and Emeritus transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Handle faculty retirement sensitively—balancing legal changes, competence concerns, incentives for retirement, and dignified treatment of retirees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of changing retirement laws and the infeasibility of selective competence testing. Use institutional incentives (golden parachutes, buyouts, two years' salary with no duties) when allowed to encourage voluntary retirement. For retirees, arrange respectful treatment: shared or retained office space, library cards, Internet access, occasional paid teaching, and Emeritus status when appropriate. Avoid forced or humiliating separations; consult legal counsel if necessary and aim for negotiated, dignified exits. Recognize some institutions (e.g., UC) have special funds enabling attractive retirement packages; others may lack such flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling tenured faculty wishing to change departmental affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate and process requests from tenured faculty to change departments (courtesy appointments, joint appointments, or full transfers) with attention to tenure, teaching, service, and administrative implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a courtesy appointment as a light-weight step (library privileges, occasional course). Joint appointments bring dual teaching/service obligations and shared oversight by two Chairs and Deans; they affect raises, travel funds, and committee duties. Full transfers require cooperation of both Chairs, the Dean, and often a faculty vote, and must be approached cautiously since tenure and departmental responsibilities are tied to a specific department. Consider long-term effects on the individual's day-to-day life and departmental resources before approving moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising outside funds and cultivating donors
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively cultivate alumni and donors to secure discretionary funds for departmental needs rather than relying solely on the university's development office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage donors directly: educate them about the department, invite them to events, build relationships, and follow up. Learn solicitation techniques (appropriate stationery, letter format, in-person cultivation) from fundraising literature or the Development Office. Understand fundraising is slow—relationships may take six months to a year to yield large gifts—but can produce significant long-term discretionary income for travel, scholarships, or endowed lectureships. Coordinate with the university's Development Office, who are experts, but take initiative rather than relying entirely on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interface with the Dean: communication and strategic framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate departmental needs to the Dean in terms the Dean values (programmatic, institutional benefits) and plan long-term hiring and resource strategies aligned with the Dean's perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the Dean manages many departments and may not understand specialized math terminology—translate needs into Dean-friendly language (impact on undergraduates, new majors, student opportunities, programmatic value). Avoid sounding self-centered; present proposals as beneficial to the College/University. Prepare five-year hiring and resource plans that account for retirements, pending tenure cases, emerging scholarly fields, medical/disability issues, and long-term objectives. Use the Executive Committee to craft Dean-oriented pitches. Anticipate administrative biases against math and proactively counter stereotypes (e.g., mathematicians as isolated or unreliable) by showing teamwork and programmatic contributions.
